title: Timing of Ocean–Atmosphere Variability and Its Impacts on Central Patagonian Ice Sheet Since MIS 3: Insights From Multiproxy Marine Records
content:
Abstract

Glaciers in southern mid-latitudes during the late Marine Isotope Stage 3 (MIS 3) were likely strongly influenced by ocean-atmosphere connections. However, the orbital- and millennial-scale variability of the Patagonian Ice Sheet (PIS) remains poorly constrained, largely due to the scarcity of terrestrial records from the western Andean margin and the limited availability of continuous, well-dated marine archives. Here, we present two continuous multiproxy marine records from the central Patagonian margin spanning the end of MIS 3 to the present. Site MD07-3119 (46°S) is influenced by proximal ice-sheet melting, whereas site MD07-3082 (49°S) reflects the broader regional evolution of the PIS. Based on a new chronological approach, our data from the two cores constrain the last maximum extent of the central western PIS to ∼26.5(+0.83)–25.5(−0.52) ka, prior to the Last Glacial Maximum defined between 24.9–19.7 ka. Furthermore, high-resolution ln(Ti/K) data and sediment accumulation rates reveal five millennial-scale events of enhanced terrestrial sediment input, with increase factors of 1.6–30, coinciding with freshwater inputs and cooling of sea surface water and interpreted as central PIS advances and retreats. These millennial-scale glacier fluctuations are synchronous with those reported for the New Zealand ice field, which may be explained by associated sea surface temperature changes and shifts of the Southern Westerly Winds, likely driven by climate variability in the South Pacific via ocean-atmosphere interactions.
